newsitem.title: USA: Columbus and IRS face off in bond case appeal.
newsitem.headline: Columbus and IRS face off in bond case appeal.

text.p: Columbus, Ohio, and the Internal Revenue Service will face off before the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, D.C., Monday in a case dealing with the tax status of a city bond issue.
Lawyers for the city and for the IRS will hold oral arguments in Columbus' appeal of a May 14 U.S. Tax Court ruling denying tax exemption for the bond issue.

Michelle Kelly-Underwood, Columbus' deputy city auditor, said the city was taking a "wait and see" attitude on how the three-judge panel would rule. She said a decision could take two to three months.
An attorney for the IRS declined to comment on the case.

Columbus filed the appeal after Tax Court Judge Theodore Tannenwald Jr refused to reconsider his May 14 ruling in fovor of the IRS' contention that bonds Columbus wants to issue to refund taxable notes it sold to pay off a pension liability would be arbitrage bonds and not eligible for tax exemption.

The city filed the lawsuit in 1995 in the wake of a 1994 IRS private letter ruling denying tax exemption for the bonds. Columbus had argued that the bond issue only represented an exchange of liability and was not motivated by arbitrage.

The road to tax court began in 1993 when Columbus won passage of a bill in the Ohio Legislature allowing municipalities to prepay their liabilities to the Ohio Police and Firemen's Disability and Pension fund in return for having those liabilities discounted by the fund.
Columbus, which owed the fund about $41.4 million, got its liability discounted to $27 million payable in a lump sum to the fund.

The city then prepared to issue $27 million of tax-exempt general obligation bonds in December 1993 to raise the money the pension fund would then be free to invest at a yield high enough to make up for the discount.
However, in a seldom seen development, the city halted the pricing of the bonds after the IRS raised last-minute concerns.
The move led five other Ohio cities to cancel plans to sell tax-free bonds to pay off their pension liabilities.

Columbus then privately placed $27 million of taxable bond anticipation notes with a money market fund and used the proceeds to pay off the pension fund liability. Those notes are due to mature Jan. 30, 1998.
If the city ultimately prevails in court, it plans to refund the notes with tax-exempt GO bonds.
